sentences: Here is Edvard Munch's The Scream.
Under a blood-red sky, a figure by a railing clasps its head in both hands.
Most people assume the figure is screaming, but according to Munch's own notes it is the other way around.
Munch made this version in 1893, in tempera and crayon on cardboard.
It was first exhibited as The Scream of Nature, part of a series he called The Frieze of Life.
Today it belongs to the National Museum of Norway in Oslo.
Start with the sky.
Bands of red and orange bend and flow like waves.
Munch wrote that he was walking at sunset with two friends when the sky suddenly turned blood-red.
Some have linked such skies to the eruption of Krakatoa, which reddened sunsets for months, though the idea is disputed.
Below it, the Oslo fjord swirls in deep blue, with two small boats on the water.
The view is identified as the one from the hill of Ekeberg, looking out over the city and the fjord.
Now come closer to the figure.
Munch wrote that he stood trembling with dread and felt an infinite scream passing through nature.
So the figure is not shouting; its hands are pressed over its ears, blocking out a sound.
The skull-like face has no hair and no sign of whether it is a man or a woman.
The eyes and nostrils are mere holes, the mouth a stretched oval.
This is not one particular person; it could be anyone.
Behind the figure, the railing cuts straight across the picture on a diagonal.
Between the bending sky and water, only this rigid line holds firm, and the contrast makes anxiety visible.
At the far end of the railing, two figures walk away.
They are often read as the two friends who, in Munch's account, walked on ahead.
On the same road, they seem untouched by what he hears.
In the red sky at upper left there is a tiny pencil note: could only have been painted by a madman.
Long thought to be a visitor's graffiti, it was confirmed in 2021, through study of the handwriting, to be Munch's own.
Munch returned to the subject in two paintings, two pastels and a lithograph of 1895.
His way of bending form and colour to follow inner feeling helped shape Expressionism, which flourished in the decades that followed.
Step back and take in the whole picture.
In Munch's telling, it is nature that screams, not the man.
Listen for a moment: what sound does this painting make for you, standing here?
